answer_1.quote: Our framework is shown in Figure . Following clinical differential diagnosis workflows , we formulate a structured reasoning framework for clinical cases. Given a clinical diagnostic instance I = {q, A}, where q represents the clinical presentation and A = {a 1 , a 2 , ..., a m } represents candidate diagnoses, the LLM generates a structured teaching reference T = {L, G} through a two-stage reasoning process, where L represents the local analysis for each clinical clue and G represents the global diagnostic synthesis respectively.
answer_1.outputs: Structured teaching references and tutoring dialogue responses

answer_2.quote: We evaluate the f1 models from the following aspects: (1) Local Clue Analysis Capability: the alignment of the decoupled local clues with teaching references using metrics Bert C and M eteor C ; the accuracy (Acc P N ) between predicted and ground-truth stances for each clue; the semantic and textual quality of reasoning explanations measured by Bert P N and M eteor P N ; the quality of clue specificity descriptions using Bert Spec and M eteor Spec ; the quality of indication description of the clue using Bert Ind and M eteor Ind ; (2) Global Synthesis and Conclusion: the final diagnosis selection accuracy Acc â; and the quality of final explanations using Bert E and M eteor E .

answer_4.quote: To validate the effectiveness of our framework, we adopt the human evaluation methodology outlined in NoteChat, which centers on simulating patient-doctor dialogues. Our evaluation incorporates both expert assessments and user experience analyses from two distinct perspectives. For evaluating the pedagogical value of Teaching References, we enlisted three experienced educators, each with over a decade of medical teaching experience. These experts evaluated 60 Teaching References, comprising 20 samples each from Phi4-14b, GPT-4o (2-shot), and the ground truth from DDxReasoning (GT). From the learning perspective, we engaged five medical students to assess the quality of local and global dialogues generated by our f2 and f3 models respectively.
answer_4.guideline: Participants ranked outputs on a 1-to-3 scale, with 1 being most preferred, using Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). Educators focused on pedagogical value and structured draft materials; students assessed dialogue quality.
